title: Teaching kids to code used to be a path to good jobs. AI has changed that.
key_facts: Launchpad Philly, a Philadelphia nonprofit, opened in 2022 to teach high school students and recent graduates coding and place them in jobs.
Entry-level tech jobs have dried up over the past year as companies cut jobs and rely on AI for basic tasks; even computer science graduates struggle to find work.
Launchpad is overhauling its curriculum to add generative AI and project-management certifications and more direct work experience, including a paid part-time business arm at $20 an hour.
Its first intensive cohort of 12 graduated last year; a year later three work full time, two are in college and the rest do freelance or part-time work.
Trainee Daniel Johnson, 20, applies to jobs about once a week and says he has not received a single reply.
Launchpad trains around 70 students at a time; staff said they 'don't know what the jobs are, what the skills are'.
quote_evidence: “I never get a single email back,” he said. “I don’t even think I’ve received a rejection.”
Now, a year later, three are working full-time, two are in college, and the rest are piecing together freelance and part-time work.
The tech industry’s job market has transformed in just the past year, with entry level jobs in particular drying up.
why_it_matters_hint: Coding was a route to good jobs for young people without college degrees; AI is closing it.
